characterList.description: Man wearing a backward purple hat and a purple shirt
characterList.name: Jeff Fritz

content_metadata.description: A guide on getting started with Visual Studio 2019, creating a simple console application in C#, and exploring available learning resources.

qAndA.answer: He adds the line `Console.ReadKey();` to his C# code.
qAndA.question: What does Jeff Fritz do to make the application wait for a key press before closing?

qAndA.answer: The console window appears briefly, displays 'Hello World!', and then immediately closes.
qAndA.question: What happens the first time Jeff Fritz runs his program?
What keyboard shortcut does Jeff Fritz use to run the program without the debugger?

qAndA.answer: He recommends checking out the Visual Studio blog on devblogs.microsoft.com and following the Visual Studio Twitch channel.
qAndA.question: Besides YouTube, where else does Jeff Fritz suggest viewers can learn about Visual Studio?

qAndA.answer: Jeff Fritz maintains a very enthusiastic and welcoming tone throughout the video. He seems genuinely excited to introduce viewers to Visual Studio and encourages them to explore its capabilities.
qAndA.question: What is the general tone and mood of Jeff Fritz's presentation?

scenes.contextualRelevance: Introduction and overview of Visual Studio 2019 features for newcomers.

narrativeProgression.description: Jeff Fritz introduces himself as a member of the Visual Studio Team
Fritz welcomes users to Visual Studio 2019
Fritz explains what users see the first time they open Visual Studio

scenes.thematicElements: Introduction to Visual Studio 2019, Getting started with Visual Studio, Options for starting a project
scenes.title: Introduction and Welcome to Visual Studio 2019

scenes.contextualRelevance: Tutorial on setting up a .NET Core Console project with Visual Studio.

keyMoments.changeDescription: The mood shifts from excited to curious as the video transitions from introduction to instructive tone.

narrativeProgression.description: Fritz proposes building a .NET Core Console Application
Fritz scrolls to the 'Create New Project' option at the bottom of the Visual Studio Start page and clicks it
Fritz chooses a template for building a console application

scenes.thematicElements: Creating a .NET Core Console Application, Using C# in Visual Studio, Understanding project templates and solutions
scenes.title: Creating a .NET Core Console Application

scenes.contextualRelevance: Detailed walkthrough of choosing templates and naming projects in Visual Studio.

narrativeProgression.description: Fritz chooses a template for building a console application

scenes.thematicElements: Selecting a Project Template, Configuring Project Settings, Initiating Project Creation
scenes.title: Navigating Project Options and Naming

scenes.contextualRelevance: Explanation of basic C# code structure and running applications within Visual Studio.

narrativeProgression.description: Fritz shows the first file created, 'Program.cs', and explains that it is a C# file
Fritz explains that the code within the file is a program class with one method: static void main
Fritz presses F5 to run the application

scenes.thematicElements: C# Code Structure, Understanding Classes and Methods, Generating Output in a Console Application
scenes.title: Understanding C# Code Structure

scenes.contextualRelevance: Troubleshooting and understanding application execution and output handling.

keyMoments.changeDescription: The sudden appearance and disappearance of console output creates momentary confusion.
Fritz's explanation clears the confusion, shifting back to curiosity.

narrativeProgression.description: Fritz presses F5 to run the application
The console application displays 'Hello World!' and then disappears
Fritz acknowledges that the application opened and closed very quickly and explains how to run it without the debugger
Fritz presses CTRL + F5 to run the application without the debugger

scenes.thematicElements: Executing the Application, Debugger Behavior, Observing Console Output
scenes.title: Executing and Observing Application Output

scenes.contextualRelevance: Enhancing program functionality with user input and flow control.

narrativeProgression.description: Fritz adds code to the application to add a prompt to press a key to continue and demonstrates the functionality

scenes.thematicElements: Adding User Interaction, Prompting for Input, Controlling Program Flow
scenes.title: Adding User Interaction to the Application

scenes.contextualRelevance: Closing remarks and motivation to explore additional Visual Studio resources.

keyMoments.changeDescription: The tone shifts from tutorial curiosity back to excitement as Fritz wraps up the lesson.

narrativeProgression.description: Fritz encourages viewers to build their own applications and points them toward resources like the Visual Studio YouTube channel, devblogs, and Twitch channel

scenes.thematicElements: Exploring Visual Studio, Building Projects, Learning Resources
scenes.title: Conclusion and Further Learning Resources

climax.description: Running the application to observe 'Hello World!' output without debugger issues.

storylines.description: The video guides viewers through the process of creating a simple 'Hello World!' console application using Visual Studio 2019, highlighting useful tips and resources for beginners.

content_metadata.title: Introduction to Visual Studio 2019 with Jeff Fritz

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hi there, my name is Jeff Fritz, and I'm a member of the Visual Studio team, and I'd like to welcome you to using Visual Studio 2019.
The first time you start Visual Studio, you're going to see a screen that looks like this behind me.
There's the left half that'll show you the list of recent projects that you've been working on.
This is the first time we've opened Visual Studio, so there's nothing here yet.
On the right side, you can choose to get started in several different ways with some existing code or even start a new project.
Or, if you really don't want to start with any code, you can click this link down at the bottom to continue without opening any code whatsoever.
Let's get started and build our first .NET Core console application using C-Sharp. I'll scroll down and choose the Create New Project option.
It'll prompt me to choose from a series of templates that are available that come as part of Visual Studio.
The one we're looking for is this one right at the top, console application with .NET Core.
It's going to be built with C-Sharp. It can run on Linux, Mac OS, or Windows, and it's a console application.
So I'll choose that and click Next. Now I can name my projects.
Let's call this first application.
That folder is fine, and the solution, the grouping of all of my projects, will just give it the same name.
And tell it to Create.
There we go. Visual Studio is opened, and there's our first file, Program C-S. You can see it here in the solution explorer on the left.
And the contents here on the right. This is a C-Sharp file. The .CS extension indicates that it contains C-Sharp program code.
This is our Program Class, and it has one method, Static Void Mean, and it takes a collection of arguments called args that are passed into it.
It does one thing. Right line to the console, Hello World.
Let's press F5 and start this application and see what happens when we run it.
Did you see it? Did you see it? It opened and closed so fast. We really couldn't see it if it was writing Hello World or not.
So here's what we're going to do. I can run this application again, but disable the debugger, and we'll see the results.

There's several different ways that I can do that. But I'm going to press Control F5, and it runs it without the debugger, and I get it saying Hello World right there above me, and press any key to continue.
Fantastic. It showed me Hello World, and it worked just fine. I can add a little bit of code right here after this console right line to actually prompt every time to press any key to continue.
I can do that by including another call to console.rightline. And take a look at this. This is called IntelliSense inside a Visual Studio.
This is Visual Studio telling us a little bit of the features that are available to us that we can use as part of the C-sharp programming language with the console object.
It's also giving us a little bit of a description as to what this method does. Right the current line terminator to the standard output stream.
So I'll just finish this. Press any key to continue.
Send me colon. And now I'll actually have it listen for any key to be pressed.
Console.read key. There we go. I'll press F5 to start it again, or I can actually click this play button up here at the top, and it'll start my application.
There it is. Hello World. Press any key to continue. And if I press any key, it finishes. And I'm returned to Visual Studio.
Alright, that's your first application here in Visual Studio 2019. What are you going to build? What do you want to know about Visual Studio going forward?
We've got a bunch of great resources for you on the Visual Studio YouTube channel. Go to youtube.com slash Visual Studio. And you can learn about all the great features that are available.

There's also fantastic blog articles for you on devblogs.microsoft.com slash Visual Studio. You can learn about some of the great features and some of the things that we have planned and that are on the road map for the next updates to Visual Studio.
Join some of the members of the Visual Studio team on weekly shows that we host on our Twitch channel. Go to twitch.tv slash Visual Studio.
And click the follow button so you can be notified every time that they go live with an additional show talking about all the great things that are going on in the Visual Studio community.
Thanks so much for watching. Best of luck to you in all the great code projects that you have ahead of you. Take care.
